To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
romantic love is associated with changes in the brain's functional organization during rest.
romantic love is associated with increased functional connectivity within the reward, emotion and motivation regulation network, and the social cognition network.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurobiology of romantic love and its effects on the brain.
the neural mechanisms of romantic experience and the underlying brain changes.
the neural mechanisms of romantic and passionate love, as it has been described by ancient Greek philosophers and poets, and by modern psychologists, and as it is experienced by many people.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

love-related changes in the human brain are associated with increased activity of reward, motivation, emotion regulation and social cognition networks, which may reflect the brain's adaptation for a close relationship with one's partner.

the present study provides first evidence that romantic love alters the brain's functional network, and that this alteration is associated with the intensity of romantic love and the duration of the relationship.
the brain's functional connectivity and regional homogeneity are altered in the romantic love state, and these alterations are associated with the intensity of love.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
romantic love is associated with changes in brain function and connectivity in reward and motivation related regions, which are likely involved in the maintenance of the relationship.

romantic love is associated with increased activity in brain regions related to reward, motivation, emotion regulation, and social cognition, and the brain regions involved in these functions may be functionally connected with one another.
romantic love can change brain function in a way that is consistent with a reward-motivation-emotion regulatory model of romantic love.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is not static and that the experience of falling in and out of love can be observed in the brain.

the neural correlates of love are different from those of attachment, which is the desire to maintain close relationships with others in general, and that love is associated with increased activity in brain areas involved in reward and emotion regulation.
the brain regions that are involved in processing romantic love are the same regions that are involved when people are thinking of the people they love.
